question: Which option is the closer architectural strategy to the anchor?

anchor.text: Gym and dining form a double-height hall on floors 2–3 above a ground-floor civic plinth of administration, medical and custodial. The classroom bar keeps special education at grade, and art, music and media share a small pavilion. Lifting assembly frees the ground for a controlled civic front and puts kitchen receiving directly below. It needs long-span transfer structure and upper-level assembly egress, and gives up media above admin.
anchor.structure: Classroom mass: academic 1-3, SPED 1 | Commons mass: gym 2-3, dining 2-3, medical 1, admin 1, custodial 1 | Third mass: art/music 1, media 2 | Direct links: classroom-commons, classroom-third

option_1.text: Both non-commons masses rise three floors. A support tower stacks administration, medical and custodial at grade, special education on floor 2 and media on top. Art and music occupy the academic bar's ground floor beneath classrooms on all three floors. This meets the three-floor, ground-floor arts and media-above-admin preferences together. In exchange, special education loses ground access, depends on elevators and protected egress, and is separated from grade-level classmates.
option_1.structure: Classroom mass: academic 1-3, art/music 1 | Commons mass: gym 1, dining 1 | Third mass: SPED 2, media 3, medical 1, admin 1, custodial 1 | Direct links: classroom-commons, classroom-third, commons-third

option_2.text: Special education is paired with administration, medical and media in a two-story support bar, keeping specialized services together. Core academic shares its bar with ground-floor arts and custodial, and that bar links to both other masses. Clustering special education with administrative and medical support helps services and supervision. It distances those students from grade-level peers, and the two-story support bar may be too small for its required width.
option_2.structure: Classroom mass: academic 1-3, art/music 1, custodial 1 | Commons mass: gym 1, dining 1 | Third mass: SPED 1-2, media 2, medical 1, admin 1 | Direct links: classroom-commons, classroom-third

anchor.text: Both non-commons masses rise three floors. A support tower stacks administration, medical and custodial at grade, special education on floor 2 and media on top. Art and music occupy the academic bar's ground floor beneath classrooms on all three floors. This meets the three-floor, ground-floor arts and media-above-admin preferences together. In exchange, special education loses ground access, depends on elevators and protected egress, and is separated from grade-level classmates.

option_1.text: Apart from the gym-dining hall, both buildings are three stories tall. One is a vertical support building: front office, nurse and maintenance at street level, the special-education suite one level up, and the library at the top. The other is the teaching bar, with art and music studios at grade and classrooms on every level. Every stated floor preference is satisfied, but students in special education have no ground-level access, rely on lifts and protected stairs, and are apart from their general-education peers.

option_2.text: Core academic stacks over a ground-floor civic front, with media on the bar's top floor. Special education and art and music share an accessible one-story wing. The commons is the third mass, and all three masses are linked to each other. Special education gets ground-level access and sits next to the arts, but is separated from general classrooms, which weakens inclusion. Two single-story masses give up the three-floor preference.

anchor.text: A single academic bar holds all classrooms, with art and music on its ground floor. A compact civic hub of administration, medical and custodial, topped by media, sits between the bar and a double-height commons. All movement between classrooms and commons passes through the civic hub. This centralizes supervision but lengthens daily lunch and gym routes. The hub and commons give up the three-floor preference.

option_1.text: Core academic stacks over a ground-floor civic front, with media on the bar's top floor. Special education and art and music share an accessible one-story wing. The commons is the third mass, and all three masses are linked to each other. Special education gets ground-level access and sits next to the arts, but is separated from general classrooms, which weakens inclusion. Two single-story masses give up the three-floor preference.

option_2.text: Every classroom is in one teaching bar whose ground level houses the art and music rooms. Between this bar and the tall gym-and-dining hall stands a small front-office block containing the principal's office, nurse and maintenance, with the library on its upper level. Students reach lunch and gym only by passing through that office block, which makes oversight easy but daily trips longer. Neither the office block nor the hall reaches three stories.

anchor.text: Gym and dining are separately enclosed double-height rooms sharing a two-sided stage, a reading of 'together' no parent uses. One long bar holds classrooms, special education and administration, with media above. Art and music, medical and custodial form a pavilion. The twin rooms allow gym class and lunch at the same time. The long consolidated bar approaches the 60-m cap, and the nurse is separated from the front office.

anchor.text: Media moves to the middle floor of the learning bar as a shared daily heart for every grade, above ground-floor special education. A one-story civic-arts front pairs administration and medical with art and music for community use. This case gives up the media-above-administration preference to make media reachable daily from classrooms. The civic-arts front also gives up the three-floor preference.

option_1.text: Special education, the nurse and administration share an accessible ground-floor welcome house, with media above. Classrooms fill two bar floors, topped by a third-floor art and music studio. Custodial serves the kitchen from inside the commons. Special education gets grade access beside the nurse and office but sits apart from grade-level classrooms. Art and music give up the ground floor for a top-lit roof studio over classrooms.

option_2.text: The library is placed on the second level of the classroom building, so every grade passes it daily; special education sits directly beneath it at grade. A single-story front building combines the office and nurse with the art and music rooms, open to community use. Putting the library among the classrooms means it is not above the office, and the front building stays one level.

anchor.text: Gym, dining and the front office form one civic mass at the main entrance, so evening community events use a single controlled door while the classroom bar can be locked off behind it.

option_1.text: For evening and weekend use, the hall and its lobby are placed in a free-standing pavilion with its own entrance and toilets; the teaching building is never opened, and staff close one gate between them.

option_2.text: Gym, dining and the front office are spread along the classroom bar at the main entrance, so evening community events pass along the main corridor and the classroom areas cannot be locked off separately.

anchor.text: The gym-dining commons sits between a learning bar and a front house. The front house holds administration, medical, art and music, and custodial, with media above. Every daily route crosses the commons, making it the school's social centre rather than an end point. Classrooms reach the office and nurse only through the commons. Assembly, lunch and gym use therefore conflict with circulation and acoustics, and with separating the academic wing after hours.
